questions.q: According to this lesson, what's the risk of treating "clicks before code" as an absolute rule?
options: It has no risk; it should always be followed without exception
It can lead to either an unreadable tangle of Flow elements, or reaching for Apex out of habit when declarative would do
It means validation rules can never be used
It requires every process to use Apex instead
questions.explain: Both failure modes are real: forcing complexity into Flow past the point of readability, or using Apex by habit when a simpler declarative tool would have worked.

questions.q: Which requirement is a validation rule or formula field best suited for?
options: Routing a record to a human for a judgment call
Evaluating fields on a record and returning true/false or a value
Calling an external system with custom authentication
Processing hundreds of thousands of records in bulk
questions.explain: Formulas are for expressible logic on data already present. Judgment calls need approval processes; integrations and bulk performance may need Apex.

questions.q: Why can't a requirement needing a human judgment call be solved with Apex code alone?
options: Apex cannot access record data
Code can evaluate data but cannot ask a person to decide something
Apex triggers only run on delete operations
Judgment calls require a validation rule instead
questions.explain: Any automated logic, declarative or code, can only evaluate data it has. A genuine decision by a person requires routing to that person, which is what an approval process does.

questions.q: Which of these is a legitimate reason to choose Apex over a declarative solution?
options: The admin personally prefers writing code
The logic needs provably correct, tested behavior across complex multi-object transactions
The requirement is a simple required-field check
The process needs to notify one specific user
questions.explain: Apex's required, enforced test coverage gives a level of verification that matters when correctness is high-stakes. Simple checks and notifications are well-served by declarative tools.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say this decision "isn't permanent"?
options: Because Salesforce deletes Apex code automatically after a year
Because Flow gains new declarative capability with each release, so a requirement that needed code before might not anymore
Because validation rules expire after 90 days
Because approval processes must be rebuilt every release
questions.explain: Salesforce ships new declarative capability several times a year, so a tool choice that was correct at one point is worth revisiting as both the requirement and the platform change.
